title: Matter
hookLine: twenty-eight kinds of matter, beginning with the four great elements

lines: THE OTHER SIDE OF THE WORLD.
cards: Press a fingertip against the table, or your knee, or the arm of the chair. Something pushes back. It's hard, or soft.
It's warm, or cool. Leave it there a moment and there's a faint press, a little give, maybe the beat of a pulse. For days this path has looked at the mind, factor by factor.
Today the Abhidhamma turns to the other side of its world: the stuff that pushes back. It has one word for all of it, and it begins its list with four.

teach.b: You met these four in the body back on day two hundred fifty-four. Today they get a closer look. The word is rupa: form, or matter.
In one sutta the Buddha plays on a verb that means to be afflicted. It's called rupa, he says, because it gets afflicted: by cold and heat, hunger and thirst, flies and mosquitoes, wind and sun.
Matter, in this telling, is the part of you that can be bitten.

The manual called the Abhidhammattha Sangaha counts twenty-eight kinds of matter, and it begins with four great elements: earth, water, fire and air. These aren't soil, rain, flame and wind. They're qualities.
Earth is hardness and softness, what pushes back. Water is cohesion, what holds a thing together and lets it flow. Fire is heat, and cold too.

Air is motion and support, the way air keeps a tire firm. Every bit of matter, the manual says, has all four, in different measure. A stone is mostly earth, yet it still holds together, has a temperature, presses.

And a strange detail: in this system, water can't be touched. Put a hand in a stream, and touch meets softness, coolness and pressure: earth, fire and air. Cohesion is known by the mind, not the skin.
The old suttas use the same four to look at the body: hair and bones as earth, blood and sweat as water, warmth as fire, breath as air.

teach.h: NOT MINE, NOT ME, NOT MY SELF.
teach.b: And of each one they say: this is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.

how: In Abhidhamma study, students learn the four great elements as qualities of matter, and in meditation some Theravada traditions teach attending to earth, water, fire and air in the body one by one.

o: a feeling, pleasant or painful, in the body
the mind that knows color, sound and touch
form, matter: what can be pressed and bitten

games.q: the four great elements: tap the pairs.

s: in the Abhidhamma, the earth element means soil
it means hardness and softness, a quality found in every bit of matter.
you can feel the water element by touch
in this system touch meets earth, fire and air. cohesion is known by the mind.
one sutta says rupa gets its name from being afflicted
by cold and heat, hunger and thirst, flies and mosquitoes, wind and sun.

games.q: you put your hand into a cool stream. by the Abhidhamma's account, what is your skin actually meeting?
o: softness, coolness and pressure: earth, fire and air
nothing at all: matter isn't real here
games.why: touch meets earth, fire and air. the water element, cohesion, is known by the mind, not by the skin.

practice: Feel the four, one at a time: earth in the weight of you on the seat, then water, the mind's sense of your body holding together as one shape.
Then fire, warmth in your hands and coolness at the tip of the nose, and air, the breath pressing the chest out and letting it settle back. If attention drifts, begin again at earth.

wordCard.voice: Rupa. Form, matter: the part of the world that can be pressed, warmed, moved and bitten, beginning with four great elements. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali and Sanskrit: form, matter. one sutta ties the name to a verb for being afflicted.

carryVoice: Your line: four great elements. Hardness, cohesion, heat and motion, in every bit of matter, your own hand included. Same time tomorrow.

sources.ref: Samyutta Nikaya 22.79 (Khajjaniya Sutta), why it is called form
